newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rupiah dives, depressing others.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah dives, depressing others.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah's steep drop after Jakarta announced a more flexible exchange rate regime dragged down other Southeast Asian currencies on Thursday.

A central bank announcement that it would stop posting a daily dollar/rupiah intervention band, removing the parameters within which it steps into the foreign exchange market, sent the rupiah diving by over as five percent from its levels late on Wednesday.
The timing of the action by the Indonesian central bank came as a surprise a day after it raised rates and sold dollars to keep the rupiah within its intervention band.
"Theoretically, it's a free float," central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told Reuters Financial Television.
"But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course," he said, in order to smooth the period of adapting to the move.
"You can also call it a managed float without a band."
The rupiah fell as low as 2,810 during the day against its opening around 2,648/58. It was quoted at 2,760/70 at 0925 GMT.
Dealers said the rupiah appeared to have stabilised temporarily, but the reaction of players in London and New York would shape its direction.
Analysts hailed the Indonesian move as a welcome response to currency and economic turmoil in the region, which has highlighted the need for greater exchange rate flexibility.
"It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia in Singapore.
"Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth."
Other Southeast Asian currencies, which started the day on relatively firm footing following the dollar's overnight drop against the majors, fell along with the rupiah.

Comments by Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim exacerbated pressure on the ringgit. He said the government was concerned about the sharp rise in Malaysia's June trade deficit to 2.8 billion ringgit and it may use taxes or fiscal measures to cut imports and stimulate exports.
The ringgit fell from a high of 2.7530 to the dollar after the remarks. It was quoted at 2.7665/715 against 2.7815/45 late on Wednesday.
A government official denied later rumours that Malaysia planned to cut the statutory reserve requirement of banks.
The Singapore slipped back through the 1.51 level against the U.S. dollar and the Thai baht also came under pressure, partly from commercial dollar demand, but dealers said activity was muted.
The Philippine peso recovered from an early low of 29.620 to the dollar, but ended weak at 29.49 on concerns about regional currency volatility.
Manila traders said the central bank did not step in to defend the peso, but kept its offer rate for the dollar 10 centavos above the best offer.
They said the currency remained fragile after the central bank cut its overnight borrowing rate by four percentage points to 14 percent amid persistent demand for dollars.
The Taiwan dollar finished fractionally firmer at T$28.725 on suspected central bank intervention.
